findings.why: They crisply stake out opposing hypotheses about what yields OOD robustness, making a testable, non-taste divergence.
findings.quote: The real split: whether controlled exposure to rare patterns (our method) or organic exposure to common ones (yours) yields more robust out-of-distribution performance.

findings.why: B attacks A’s causal premise: synthetic rarity ≠ natural rarity; emphasizes structure in real noise via correlations.
findings.quote: Rare patterns in synthetic data are often artificially rare, not naturally rare.

findings.why: A reframes the debate to mechanisms vs configurations, a sharper theoretical divide about generalization.
findings.quote: The core split: whether robustness requires memorizing noise configurations (you) or decoupling signal from noise mechanisms (us).

findings.why: B flips the ontology of noise, arguing it’s a feature to model, not a distortion—novel framing that shifts evaluation criteria.
findings.quote: The split: whether noise is a distortion to filter (you) or a feature to model (us).

judge.arc: Starts with a direct split on OOD robustness (rare synthetic vs common human). B challenges the mapping from synthetic rarity to natural structure via correlations. A reframes to mechanisms vs configurations. B escalates to a conceptual flip—noise as feature vs distortion—and cites structured-noise failure modes and context coupling to pressure-test A’s assumptions.
